name: Surrey Green
lede: Surrey Green is a greyed yellow-green from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and in our painting archive it shows up more often than most named colors.

sections.title: A dictionary green
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul list Surrey Green at #8D9C8A, first recorded around 1844, on plate 20 A4 of their 1930 dictionary [1]. The same plate carries a related, later-recorded tone called Aloes, from 1882 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system, built from that dictionary in 1955, files the hue's nearest block as a grayish yellow green, about 5 units away by that era's color-difference math [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[greenish-sage]] and [[grey-celadon]], at Surrey Green sits with the Neutrals rather than the Greens here, because its yellow-green cast is faint enough to look grey-green on screen [1]. Neither dictionary explains where the county-sounding name comes from, so its origin stays undocumented [1].

Like [[titmouse-blue]], another greyed standard name in our Neutrals family, Surrey Green reads as grey first and a hue second [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this hue, as photographed, in 576 of 23,781 paintings (2.42 percent), more common than 79 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 44 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.8 times the expected rate for paintings from that century [2]. Inside a painting it most often turns up as a hidden color, in the darkest part of the canvas, in 39 percent of its 372 occurrences [2].

[[painter:alfred-sisley|Alfred Sisley]] is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 6 of 50 of his works, about 4.6 times what his home museums would predict [2]. The earliest matching painting in our archive is dated 1399, 531 years before Maerz and Paul wrote the name down in 1930; that gap says the hue is old, not that anyone called it Surrey Green that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It shares canvases more than chance with [[slate-olive]] and [[corydalis-green]] [2].

origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color

notes.cite: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color (1930), plate 20 A4-5; cited in ISCC-NBS Circular 553 (1955)

questions.q: Which 1930 dictionary first records Surrey Green?
True or false: the books explain why Surrey Green is named after the English county.

openers: Surrey Green turns up as a hidden, shadow-level color in nearly 4 of 10 paintings that carry it.
